claim: Nup98 is a mobile component of the nuclear pore complex (NPC).
source: Nup98 is a mobile component of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) (Griffis et al., 2002; Rabut et al., 2004; Oka et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Griffis et al., 2002; Rabut et al., 2004; Oka et al., 2010).

claim: Nup98 is essential for selective nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: Nup98 is essential for such fundamental functions of NPC as selective nucleocytoplasmic transport (Radu et al., 1995; Powers et al., 1997; Zolotukhin and Felber, 1999; Oka et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Radu et al., 1995; Powers et al., 1997; Zolotukhin and Felber, 1999; Oka et al., 2010).

claim: Nup98 is essential for maintenance of the permeability barrier.
source: Nup98 is essential for such fundamental functions of NPC as selective nucleocytoplasmic transport (Radu et al., 1995; Powers et al., 1997; Zolotukhin and Felber, 1999; Oka et al., 2010) and maintenance of the permeability barrier (Hulsmann et al., 2012; Laurell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Hulsmann et al., 2012; Laurell et al., 2011).

claim: Nup98 is involved in gene regulation.
source: it has been shown that Nup98 is involved in gene regulation (Capelson et al., 2010; Kalverda et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2013; Light et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Capelson et al., 2010; Kalverda et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2013; Light et al., 2013).

claim: Nup98 is involved in posttranscriptional regulation of specific sets of messenger RNAs (mRNAs).
source: posttranscriptional regulation of specific sets of messenger RNAs (mRNAs) (Singer et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Singer et al., 2012).

claim: Nup98 is involved in mitotic spindle assembly.
source: mitotic spindle assembly (Cross and Powers, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Cross and Powers, 2011).

claim: Nup98 is involved in mitotic checkpoint.
source: mitotic checkpoint (Jeganathan et al., 2005; Salsi et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Jeganathan et al., 2005; Salsi et al., 2014).

claim: Nup98 is involved in NPC disassembly.
source: NPC disassembly (Laurell et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Laurell et al., 2011).

claim: Nup98-fusions consist of N-terminal half of Nup98 containing multiple phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats and C-terminus of various partner proteins.
source: Nup98-fusions, which consist of N-terminal half of Nup98 containing multiple phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats and C-terminus of various partner proteins (Gough et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Gough et al., 2011).

claim: More than 30 different proteins with various physiological functions have been reported as Nup98 fusion partners.
source: More than 30 different proteins with various physiological functions have been reported as Nup98 fusion partners (reviewed in (Gough et al., 2011))
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review (Gough et al., 2011).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 results from t(7;11)(p15;p15) chromosomal translocation associated with acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and chronic myeloid leukemia.
source: Nup98-HoxA9 is one of the most frequent Nup98-fusion resulting from t(7;11)(p15;p15) chromosomal translocation associated with acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and chronic myeloid leukemia (Nakamura et al., 1996; Borrow et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Nakamura et al., 1996; Borrow et al., 1996; Nishiyama et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2000).

claim: Ectopic expression of Nup98-HoxA9 induces leukemia in mice.
source: the ectopic expression of Nup98-HoxA9 induces leukemia in mice (Kroon et al., 2001; Iwasaki et al., 2005; Dash et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Kroon et al., 2001; Iwasaki et al., 2005; Dash et al., 2002).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 inhibits hematopoietic cell differentiation.
source: Nup98-HoxA9 inhibits hematopoietic cell differentiation (Kroon et al., 2001; Calvo et al., 2002; Takeda et al., 2006; Chung et al., 2006; Yassin et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to five published studies (Kroon et al., 2001; Calvo et al., 2002; Takeda et al., 2006; Chung et al., 2006; Yassin et al., 2009).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 enhances symmetric division of hematopoietic precursor cells in vitro.
source: enhances symmetric division of hematopoietic precursor cells in vitro(Wu et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Wu et al., 2007).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 contributes to leukemogenesis most likely by impairing cellular differentiation.
source: suggesting that Nup98-HoxA9 contributes to leukemogenesis most likely by impairing cellular differentiation
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited studies showing inhibition of differentiation and enhancement of symmetric division.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 acts as a transcriptional regulator.
source: Nup98-HoxA9 was shown to act as a transcriptional regulator (Kasper et al., 1999; Ghannam et al., 2004; Bei et al., 2005; Yassin et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Kasper et al., 1999; Ghannam et al., 2004; Bei et al., 2005; Yassin et al., 2009).

claim: Ectopic expression of Nup98-HoxA9 causes upregulation, rather than downregulation, of numerous genes.
source: genome-wide gene expression analysis revealed that ectopic expression of Nup98-HoxA9 causes upregulation, rather than downregulation, of numerous genes (Ghannam et al., 2004; Takeda et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Ghannam et al., 2004; Takeda et al., 2006).

claim: The FG repeat of Nup98 associates with CREB-binding protein (CBP)/p300.
source: the FG repeat of Nup98 is known to associate with CREB-binding protein (CBP)/p300 (Kasper et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Kasper et al., 1999).

claim: CBP/p300 is a histone acetyltransferase that functions as a transcriptional co-activator.
source: CREB-binding protein (CBP)/p300 (Kasper et al., 1999), a histone acetyltransferase that functions as a transcriptional co-activator
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CBP/p300 function.

claim: The FG repeat of Nup98 associates with histone deacetylase (HDAC) 1.
source: histone deacetylase (HDAC) 1 (Bai et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Bai et al., 2006).

claim: The interaction of Nup98 FG repeats with p300 by itself is not sufficient to promote self-renewal of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: However, the interaction of Nup98 FG repeats with p300 by itself is not sufficient to promote self-renewal of hematopoietic stem cells (Yung et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Yung et al., 2011).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 is specifically recruited to the vicinity of Hox cluster genes via chromosomally bound Crm1.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Nup98-HoxA9 is specifically recruited to the vicinity of Hox cluster genes via chromosomally bound Crm1, a nuclear export factor that was originally identified as a protein required for maintaining the chromosomal structure in yeast (Adachi and Yanagida, 1989), to activate Hox cluster regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (ChIP-seq analysis) and citation to the original identification of Crm1 (Adachi and Yanagida, 1989).

claim: Crm1 was originally identified as a protein required for maintaining the chromosomal structure in yeast.
source: Crm1, a nuclear export factor that was originally identified as a protein required for maintaining the chromosomal structure in yeast (Adachi and Yanagida, 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Adachi and Yanagida, 1989).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 fusion protein localizes as distinct small dots in the nucleus.
source: Previous reports have demonstrated that Nup98-HoxA9 fusion protein localizes as distinct small dots in the nucleus (Kasper et al., 1999; Bai et al., 2006; Xu and Powers, 2010; Oka et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Kasper et al., 1999; Bai et al., 2006; Xu and Powers, 2010; Oka et al., 2010).

claim: EGFP-tagged Nup98-HoxA9 was easily distinguished as small nuclear dots when expressed in HeLa cells.
source: When expressed in HeLa cells, the enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP)-tagged Nup98-HoxA9 was easily distinguished as small nuclear dots.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nup98 FG repeats were detected as large dots mostly associated with the nucleolus.
source: Nup98 FG repeats were detected as large dots mostly associated with the nucleolus
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 1A, consistent with earlier reports (Oka et al., 2010; Xu and Powers, 2010).

claim: HoxA9-Ct showed an even nucleoplasmic distribution.
source: HoxA9 C-terminus containing the homeodomain, HoxA9-Ct, showed an even nucleopolasmic distribution (Figure 1A), consistent with earlier reports (Oka et al., 2010; Xu and Powers, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 1A, consistent with earlier reports (Oka et al., 2010; Xu and Powers, 2010).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 dots were frequently adjacent to DAPI-dense heterochromatin regions.
source: We noticed that Nup98-HoxA9 dots were not randomly localized within the nucleus, but were frequently adjacent to 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-dense heterochromatin regions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) as revealed by co-staining with DAPI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 dots were frequently associated with H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, facultative heterochromatin markers.
source: Furthermore, immunocytochemical analysis using monoclonal antibodies specific to histone modifications (Kimura et al., 2008) (Figure 1C) revealed that those dots were frequently associated with H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, facultative heterochromatin markers (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citations to published studies (Kimura et al., 2008; Trojer and Reinberg, 2007).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 dots were not associated with the marker for constitutive heterochromatin H3K9me3.
source: but not with the marker for constitutive heterochromatin H3K9me3 (Peters et al., 2003, Rice et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citations to published studies (Peters et al., 2003, Rice et al., 2003).

claim: H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are facultative heterochromatin markers.
source: H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, facultative heterochromatin markers (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007).

claim: H3K9me3 is a marker for constitutive heterochromatin.
source: the marker for constitutive heterochromatin H3K9me3 (Peters et al., 2003, Rice et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Peters et al., 2003, Rice et al., 2003).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 dots are not randomly positioned in the nucleus but are associated with specific chromatin domains.
source: These results indicate that Nup98-HoxA9 dots are not randomly positioned in the nucleus but are associated with specific chromatin domains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing association with specific histone modifications.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 nuclear dots in ES cells were fewer in number and more heterogeneous in size compared with dots revealed in HeLa cells or NIH 3T3 cells.
source: We found that although Nup98-HoxA9 nuclear dots could also be observed in ES cells, they were fewer in number and more heterogeneous in size compared with dots revealed in HeLa cells or NIH 3T3 cells (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Immunocytochemical analysis in ES cells showed the partial co-localization of Nup98-HoxA9 dots with H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, but less with H3K9me3.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis in ES cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) also showed the partial co-localization of Nup98-HoxA9 dots with H3K9me2 and H3K27me3, but less with H3K9me3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intranuclear distribution of Nup98-HoxA9 changes depending on the cell type.
source: These findings indicated that the intranuclear distribution of Nup98-HoxA9 indeed changes depending on the cell type
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing different localization patterns in different cell types.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 might be involved in a cell type-specific gene and/or chromatin regulation.
source: Together, these results suggested that Nup98-HoxA9 might be involved in a cell type-specific gene and/or chromatin regulation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed cell type-specific localization patterns.

claim: FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 had a similar localization pattern to transiently expressed EGFP-Nup98-HoxA9 in ES cells.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis using stable ES clones demonstrated that FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 had a similar localization pattern to transiently expressed EGFP-Nup98-HoxA9 in ES cells (Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was not overexpressed compared with endogenous Nup98.
source: Immunoblotting using monoclonal antibody that is raised against the N-terminal (A.A. 1–466) of Nup98 (Fukuhara et al., 2005) revealed that FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was not overexpressed compared with endogenous Nup98 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to the antibody source (Fukuhara et al., 2005).

claim: FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 expressing stable ES cell clones had distinct flat colonies.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 expressing stable ES cell clones (Nup98-HoxA9 ES) had distinct flat colonies, which was in contrast to tighter colonies of spherical shape detected in parental ES, Nup98FG, or HoxA9-Ct expressing ES cells (Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells expressed stem cell marker genes.
source: Further experiments revealed that Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells expressed stem cell marker genes
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown in detail).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells had proliferation rates comparable to those of parental ES cells.
source: and had proliferation rates comparable to those of parental ES cells
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown in detail).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells were not differentiated.
source: indicating that they were not differentiated (data not shown)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the expression of stem cell markers and normal proliferation rates.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells show more resistance to spontaneous cell differentiation in the absence of leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), compared with parental ES, Nup98FG, or HoxA9-Ct expressing ES clones.
source: In addition, Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells show more resistance to spontaneous cell differentiation in the absence of leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), compared with parental ES, Nup98FG, or HoxA9-Ct expressing ES clones (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A small fraction of genes (less than 1%) were strongly induced (more than 10-fold) in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells compared with their expression levels in parental or HoxA9-Ct ES cells.
source: We found that a small fraction of genes (less than 1%) were strongly induced (more than 10-fold) in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells compared with their expression levels in parental or HoxA9-Ct ES cells (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA microarray analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Hox cluster genes were highly activated in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that Hox cluster genes were highly activated in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells (Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA microarray analysis data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: More than a half of the top 32 upregulated genes, which were common in both of Nup98-HoxA9 clone #1 and Nup98-HoxA9 clone #9, were Hox cluster genes belonging to Hox-A, -B, and -C clusters.
source: In particular, more than a half of the top 32 upregulated genes, which were common in both of Nup98-HoxA9 clone #1 and Nup98-HoxA9 clone #9, were Hox cluster genes belonging to Hox-A, -B, and -C clusters (Table 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA microarray analysis data shown in Table 1.

claim: Upregulation of Hox cluster genes in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells was validated by reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).
source: which were validated by reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) (Figure 2G)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is a good correlation between the intranuclear distribution of Nup98-HoxA9 and its function in transcription.
source: These results suggest that there is a good correlation between the intranuclear distribution of Nup98-HoxA9 and its function in transcription, since Hox gene cluster regions are known to be organized as facultative heterochromatin (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and citation to a published study (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007).

claim: Hox gene cluster regions are known to be organized as facultative heterochromatin.
source: since Hox gene cluster regions are known to be organized as facultative heterochromatin (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007).

claim: FG repeat domains of hNup153 and hNup214 have been demonstrated to be functionally exchangeable with Nup98 FG repeats in experiments that addressed the transforming ability in NIH3T3 cells.
source: Therefore, we created chimeric Nup-fusions by replacing Nup98 FG repeats with those from hNup153FG (A.A.1118–1475) and hNup214FG (A.A.1605–2090), which have been demonstrated to be functionally exchangeable in experiments that addressed the transforming ability in NIH3T3 cells (Kasper et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Kasper et al., 1999).

claim: Nup153-HoxA9 and Nup214-HoxA9 were not distributed as distinct fine nuclear dots observed in the case of the Nup98-HoxA9 fusion.
source: When these chimeric proteins (Nup153-HoxA9 and Nup214-HoxA9) were expressed in HeLa cells, they were not distributed as distinct fine nuclear dots observed in the case of the Nup98-HoxA9 fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), in agreement with a previous report (Xu and Powers, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to a published study (Xu and Powers, 2013).

claim: In contrast to Nup98-HoxA9, other Nup-fusions were distributed more evenly in the nucleus.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, we found that, in contrast to the case with Nup98-HoxA9, other Nup-fusions were distributed more evenly in the nucleus (although note that a few dots within the nucleus were seen with the Nup214-HoxA9 fusion)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of Nup153-HoxA9 or Nup214-HoxA9 did not affect the expression of Hox cluster genes.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the expression of Nup153-HoxA9 or Nup214-HoxA9 did not affect the expression of Hox cluster genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Substantial numbers of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies of Nup153-HoxA9-expressing ES cells were observed in the absence of LIF.
source: Of note, we constantly observed substantial numbers of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies of Nup153-HoxA9-expressing ES cells in the absence of LIF (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observation of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies of Nup153-HoxA9-expressing ES cells in the absence of LIF may be related to the function of Nup153 in maintaining stem cell pluripotency in ES cells.
source: which may be related to the function of Nup153 in maintaining stem cell pluripotency in ES cells, as demonstrated in a recent study (Jacinto et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and citation to a published study (Jacinto et al., 2015).

claim: HoxA9 expression did not induce the activation of Hox cluster genes.
source: Gene expression analysis revealed that HoxA9 expression did not induce the activation of Hox cluster genes (Figure 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: These results underscore the physiological significance of Nup98 FG repeats in the dysregulation of Hox cluster gene expression.
source: These results underscore the physiological significance of Nup98 FG repeats in the dysregulation of Hox cluster gene expression.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing that only Nup98-HoxA9, but not other Nup-fusions or HoxA9 alone, activates Hox genes.

claim: Ectopic expression of Nup98-HoxA9 in HeLa cells caused sequestration of nucleoplasmic and nuclear envelope-localized Crm1 on Nup98-HoxA9 dots within the nucleus.
source: Indeed, the ectopic expression of Nup98-HoxA9 in HeLa cells caused sequestration of nucleoplasmic and nuclear envelope-localized Crm1 on Nup98-HoxA9 dots within the nucleus (Figure 4A, top)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4A, top.

claim: Partial recruitment of Crm1 to FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 dots was observed in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells.
source: When we stained Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells, we also noticed partial recruitment of Crm1 to FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 dots (Figure 4A, bottom)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4A, bottom.

claim: Treatment with leptomycin B (LMB) causes a dynamic redistribution of Nup98 nuclear dots.
source: We have previously demonstrated that treatment with leptomycin B (LMB), a specific inhibitor of the cargo binding of Crm1 (Kudo et al., 1998), causes a dynamic redistribution of Nup98 nuclear dots (Oka et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kudo et al., 1998; Oka et al., 2010).

claim: LMB is a specific inhibitor of the cargo binding of Crm1.
source: leptomycin B (LMB), a specific inhibitor of the cargo binding of Crm1 (Kudo et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Kudo et al., 1998).

claim: Nup98-Crm1 association is dependent on the cargo binding status of Crm1.
source: This finding indicated that Nup98-Crm1 association is dependent on the cargo binding status of Crm1
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that LMB treatment causes redistribution of Nup98 dots.

claim: When Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells were treated with LMB for 2 hr, the dots disappeared.
source: When Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells were treated with LMB for 2 hr, the dots disappeared (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The disappearance of Nup98-HoxA9 dots upon LMB treatment was concomitant with a modest decrease in the protein level.
source: The disappearance of dots was concomitant with a modest decrease in the protein level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: LMB treatment did not affect the localization of full-length HoxA9, Nup153-HoxA9, and the majority of Nup214-HoxA9.
source: In contrast, LMB treatment did not affect the localization of full-length HoxA9, Nup153-HoxA9, and the majority of Nup214-HoxA9, except for a few nuclear dots of Nup214-HoxA9 that disappeared upon LMB treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Crm1 plays a critical role in the maintenance of Nup98-HoxA9 dots in ES cells.
source: These results indicate that Crm1 plays a critical role in the maintenance of Nup98-HoxA9 dots in ES cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing that LMB treatment causes disappearance of Nup98-HoxA9 dots.

claim: LMB treatment caused a significant downregulation of Hox cluster genes in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, LMB treatment caused a significant downregulation of Hox cluster genes
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: LMB treatment did not affect the expression of Oct4 and Nanog in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells.
source: while the expression of other genes, such as Oct4 and Nanog, was not much affected
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The interaction of Nup98-HoxA9 with Crm1 is necessary for the selective Hox gene activation.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that the interaction of Nup98-HoxA9 with Crm1 is necessary for the selective Hox gene activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing that LMB treatment, which disrupts Crm1 function, causes downregulation of Hox genes.

claim: A strong accumulation of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was found on chromosomal regions of four Hox clusters, Hox-A, B, C, and D.
source: Interestingly, we found a strong accumulation of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 on chromosomal regions of four Hox clusters, Hox-A, B, C, and D.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Three Hox clusters (Hox-A, Hox-B and Hox-C) showed the highest peaks in the whole genome.
source: Especially, three of these, Hox-A, Hox-B and Hox-C cluster regions showed the highest peaks in the whole genome (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Hox-A cluster region showed a single dominant peak in chromosome 6.
source: In particular, the Hox-A cluster region showed a single dominant peak in chromosome 6 (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Examination of individual Hox cluster regions revealed a selective accumulation of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 in the four Hox cluster regions.
source: Examination of individual Hox cluster regions further revealed a selective accumulation of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 in the four Hox cluster regions (Figure 5D)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Most of the genes in the Hox-D cluster were not upregulated by Nup98-HoxA9.
source: It is noteworthy that, as most of the genes in the Hox-D cluster were not upregulated by Nup98-HoxA9, the significance of its binding to this region remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the microarray data.

claim: ChIP-qPCR analysis confirmed that a significantly increased amount of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was bound to the Hox-A cluster.
source: ChIP-qPCR (quantitative polymerase chain reaction) analysis (Figure 5E) confirmed that a significantly increased amount of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was bound to the Hox-A cluster
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was not bound to the restricted regions, as represented by the intergenic region (between HoxA2 and HoxA3), promoter (HoxA4), or 5'UTR (HoxA9) regions of Hox-A cluster genes.
source: but not to the restricted regions, as represented by the intergenic region (between HoxA2 and HoxA3), promoter (HoxA4), or 5'UTR (HoxA9) regions of Hox-A cluster genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In parental ES cells, the endogenous Crm1 bound to all Hox regions including Hox-A, B, C, and D.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that in parental ES cells, the endogenous Crm1 bound to all Hox regions including Hox-A, B, C, and D (Figure 5B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Crm1 binding sites in parental ES cells were almost the same sites as those occupied by Nup98-HoxA9.
source: which were almost the same sites as those occupied by Nup98-HoxA9
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The binding of Crm1 to Hox cluster regions was significantly elevated in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells.
source: Moreover, the binding of Crm1 to Hox cluster regions was significantly elevated in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells (Figure 5B–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: LMB treatment induced a drastic decrease of Nup98-HoxA9 binding to Hox clusters.
source: Furthermore, LMB treatment induced a drastic decrease of Nup98-HoxA9 binding to Hox clusters (Figure 5B–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 forms higher order nuclear structures containing Crm1 on Hox cluster regions to induce Hox gene activation.
source: These results indicate that Nup98-HoxA9 forms higher order nuclear structures containing Crm1 on Hox cluster regions to induce Hox gene activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing co-localization and co-binding of Nup98-HoxA9 and Crm1 at Hox clusters.

claim: The peak of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 binding site was severely diminished but not shifted by LMB treatment.
source: Aggregation plot revealed that the peak of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 binding site was severely diminished but not shifted by LMB treatment (Figure 6A, left top)
evidence: The claim is supported by aggregation plot analysis shown in Figure 6A, left top.

claim: FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was preferentially targeted to the chromatin sites that originally bound Crm1 (the Crm1 binding site in control ES cells).
source: Furthermore, FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 was preferentially targeted to the chromatin sites that originally bound Crm1 (the Crm1 binding site in control ES cells) (Figure 6A, right top)
evidence: The claim is supported by aggregation plot analysis shown in Figure 6A, right top.

claim: The peak of Crm1 binding was not shifted, but rather significantly enhanced by the expression of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9.
source: Aggregation plots of the Crm1 binding signal revealed that the peak of Crm1 binding was not shifted, but rather significantly enhanced by the expression of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 (Figure 6A, left bottom)
evidence: The claim is supported by aggregation plot analysis shown in Figure 6A, left bottom.

claim: The Crm1 signal accumulated at the FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 binding site.
source: In addition, the Crm1 signal also accumulated at the FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 binding site (Figure 6A, right bottom)
evidence: The claim is supported by aggregation plot analysis shown in Figure 6A, right bottom.

claim: Statistical analyses confirmed the results from aggregation plots.
source: Statistical analyses confirmed these results (Figure 6B)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The number of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 target genes was severely decreased by LMB treatment.
source: As expected, the number of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 target genes was severely decreased by LMB treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, top left)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1, top left.

claim: The number of Crm1 target genes were significantly increased by the expression of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9.
source: On the other hand, the number of Crm1 target genes were significantly increased by the expression of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of Crm1 target genes in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells were not overlapping with FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 target genes.
source: however, the majority of these genes were not overlapping (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, top right)
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 first binds to chromatin loci where Crm1 is not present, and then, Crm1 is recruited to FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9-bound sites.
source: In these regions, it is likely that FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 first binds to chromatin loci where Crm1 is not present, and then, Crm1 is recruited to FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9-bound sites
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ChIP-seq data showing increased Crm1 binding at sites near Hox clusters where FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 binds.

claim: Both chromatin-bound Crm1 and FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 can recruit each other.
source: Therefore, these results demonstrate that both chromatin-bound Crm1 and FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 can recruit each other.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing mutual recruitment at different genomic locations.

claim: TSA treatment caused a drastic redistribution of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9, a significant increase in the number and a significant decrease in the size of dots.
source: While most of these agents only showed a minor effect on the localization pattern of Nup98-HoxA9 (Figure 7A), trichostatin A (TSA) treatment caused a drastic redistribution of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9, a significant increase in the number and a significant decrease in the size of dots, which mimicked that observed in HeLa cells (Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: TSA treatment caused redistribution of endogenous Crm1 concomitant with the redistribution of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9.
source: concomitant with the redistribution of endogenous Crm1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TSA treatment caused an upregulation of the FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 protein and mRNA.
source: We also confirmed that TSA treatment caused an upregulation of the FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 protein and mRNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Upregulation of FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 by TSA treatment occurred presumably due to the reactivation of partially silenced transgenes cloned in the Tol2 transposon vector.
source: which occurred presumably due to the reactivation of partially silenced transgenes cloned in the Tol2 transposon vector
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and knowledge about transgene silencing.

claim: A similar phenomenon of transgene reactivation by TSA was also observed in the case of transgenes created by the Sleeping Beauty transposon.
source: A similar phenomenon was also observed in the case of transgenes created by the Sleeping Beauty transposon (Garrison et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Garrison et al., 2007).

claim: Despite the increase in the FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 protein level, TSA treatment caused a drastic decrease in the binding of Nup98-HoxA9 and Crm1 to chromatin.
source: Unexpectedly, despite the increase in the FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 protein level, TSA treatment caused a drastic decrease in the binding of Nup98-HoxA9 and Crm1 to chromatin (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: TSA treatment caused a decrease in the binding of Nup98-HoxA9 and Crm1 to Hox cluster regions.
source: which was also obvious in Hox cluster regions (Figure 5B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The binding of endogenous Crm1 to Hox-A cluster in control ES cells was sensitive to TSA treatment.
source: Furthermore, our ChIP-qPCR analysis showed that the binding of endogenous Crm1 to Hox-A cluster in control ES cells was also sensitive to TSA treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Treatment of ES cells with TSA at a concentration of 50 nM drastically affects bivalent histone modifications H3K4me3 (upregulation) and H3K27me3 (downregulation), in addition to the acetylation.
source: Interestingly, it is known that treatment of ES cells with TSA at a concentration of 50 nM drastically affects bivalent histone modifications H3K4me3 (upregulation) and H3K27me3 (downregulation), in addition to the acetylation (Karantzali et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Karantzali et al., 2008).

claim: Bivalent histone marks are critical for the regulation of Hox cluster genes in ES cells.
source: Since bivalent histone marks are critical for the regulation of Hox cluster genes in ES cells (Mikkelsen et al., 2007, Pan et al., 2007, Zhao et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Mikkelsen et al., 2007, Pan et al., 2007, Zhao et al., 2007).

claim: TSA treatment caused a moderate upregulation of H3K4me3 and a robust decrease of H3K27me3 on the promoter region of Hox-A cluster genes.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4, TSA treatment caused a moderate upregulation of H3K4me3 and a robust decrease of H3K27me3 on the promoter region of Hox-A cluster genes, which is in line with a previous report (Karantzali et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and citation to a published study (Karantzali et al., 2008).

claim: Inactive histone marks, including H3K27me3, are important for the recruitment of Crm1 and FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 to the Hox-A cluster region.
source: These results suggest that inactive histone marks, including H3K27me3, are important for the recruitment of Crm1 and FLAG-Nup98-HoxA9 to the Hox-A cluster region.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing that TSA treatment, which decreases H3K27me3, also decreases Crm1 and Nup98-HoxA9 binding.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells exhibited significantly higher levels of H3K4me3, an active histone modification, in all tested Hox regions.
source: We revealed that Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells exhibited significantly higher levels of H3K4me3, an active histone modification, in all tested Hox regions (Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Enhanced levels of H3K27me3 were significant only on the HoxA9 5'UTR exon in Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells.
source: On the other hand, enhanced levels of H3K27me3 were significant only on the HoxA9 5'UTR exon (Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The binding of both S5P (initiating) and S2P (elongating) forms of RNAPII to the Hox-A cluster regions increased in the Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells compared with parental ES cells.
source: Furthermore, ChIP-qPCR analysis of phospho-CTD isoforms of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) revealed that the binding of both S5P (initiating) and S2P (elongating) forms of RNAPII to the Hox-A cluster regions increased in the Nup98-HoxA9 ES cells compared with parental ES cells (Figure 7D)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Crm1 may associate with Hox genes via inactive histone marks, such as H3K27me3.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that Crm1 may associate with Hox genes via inactive histone marks, such as H3K27me3
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 may form a local higher order chromatin structure on Crm1 binding sites to further recruit active histone modifier(s) and RNAPII to induce a selective upregulation of Hox genes.
source: and subsequently, Nup98-HoxA9 may form a local higher order chromatin structure on Crm1 binding sites to further recruit active histone modifier(s) and RNAPII to induce a selective upregulation of Hox genes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Activation of several Hox genes by Nup98-HoxA9 has been previously reported in other types of cells.
source: Although activation of several Hox genes by Nup98-HoxA9 has been previously reported in other types of cells (Calvo et al., 2002; Takeda et al., 2006; Ghannam et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Calvo et al., 2002; Takeda et al., 2006; Ghannam et al., 2004).

claim: Previous reports of Hox gene activation by Nup98-HoxA9 in other cell types showed relatively weak and not highly specific effects.
source: those effects were relatively weak and not highly specific, which is in contrast to the pronounced changes observed in our present study
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with cited studies and the current study's results.

claim: The chromatin structure, epigenetic status or chromatin-bound protein complexes of Hox cluster regions may be dissimilar in different cell types, causing varying susceptibility to Nup98-HoxA9-mediated chromatin modifications.
source: First, the chromatin structure, epigenetic status or chromatin-bound protein complexes of Hox cluster regions may be dissimilar in different cell types, causing varying susceptibility to Nup98-HoxA9-mediated chromatin modifications.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference to explain the observed cell type-specific effects.

claim: The association status of Crm1 with Hox cluster gene loci may be differentially modulated in different cell types, causing cell type-specific variability in the Nup98-HoxA9-mediated gene expression.
source: Second, the association status of Crm1 with Hox cluster gene loci, which is a prerequisite for the selective deregulation of Hox cluster genes, may be differentially modulated in different cell types, causing cell type-specific variability in the Nup98-HoxA9-mediated gene expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference to explain the observed cell type-specific effects.

claim: FG repeats of Nup153 and Nup214 are known to interact with Crm1.
source: Notably, although both FG repeats of Nup153 and Nup214 are known to interact with Crm1 (Roloff et al., 2013; Nakielny et al., 1999; Fornerod et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Roloff et al., 2013; Nakielny et al., 1999; Fornerod et al., 1997).

claim: Nup153-HoxA9 and Nup214-HoxA9 fusions failed to activate Hox cluster genes.
source: we found that these fusions, Nup153-HoxA9 and Nup214-HoxA9, failed to activate Hox cluster genes
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ability of Nup98 FG repeats to form nuclear dot-like structures is critical in Hox gene activation.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the ability of Nup98 FG repeats to form nuclear dot-like structures is critical in Hox gene activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations showing that only Nup98-HoxA9, which forms dots, activates Hox genes.

claim: The interaction of Nup98-HoxA9 with prebound Crm1 induces the alteration of chromatin structures specifically on Hox cluster regions.
source: We propose a model whereby the interaction of Nup98-HoxA9 with prebound Crm1 induces the alteration of chromatin structures specifically on Hox cluster regions
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The alteration of chromatin structures on Hox cluster regions causes robust activation of gene expression.
source: and this modification, in turn, causes robust activation of gene expression
evidence: The claim is part of the proposed model based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Hox clusters in ES cells harbor a distinctive long-range histone modification signature called the bivalent motif, which possesses both transcriptionally active H3K4me3 and repressive H3K27me3 marks.
source: It is known that Hox clusters in ES cells harbor a distinctive long-range histone modification signature called the bivalent motif, which possesses both transcriptionally active H3K4me3 and repressive H3K27me3 marks (Bernstein et al., 2006; Mikkelsen et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Bernstein et al., 2006; Mikkelsen et al., 2007).

claim: The bivalent motif is maintained through the activity of polycomb complexes.
source: This modification is maintained through the activity of polycomb complexes (Schwartz and Pirrotta, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Schwartz and Pirrotta, 2007).

claim: TSA treatment results in a robust decrease of the H3K27me3 mark on Hox cluster genes.
source: Our results demonstrate that Nup98-HoxA9/Crm1 binding to Hox region is sensitive to TSA treatment, which results in a robust decrease of the H3K27me3 mark on Hox cluster genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The expression of Nup98-HoxA9 causes a significant increase of the active histone mark H3K4me3 on Hox cluster region genes.
source: Moreover, the expression of Nup98-HoxA9 causes a significant increase of the active histone mark H3K4me3 on Hox cluster region genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The FG repeat region of Nup98 interacts with histone acetyltransferases CBP and p300.
source: Previously, it was reported that the FG repeat region of Nup98 interacts with histone acetyltransferases CBP and p300 (Kasper et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Kasper et al., 1999).

claim: MBD-R2/NSL and Trx histone modifying complexes have been demonstrated to interact with full-length Nup98 in fly.
source: In addition, MBD-R2/NSL and Trx histone modifying complexes have been demonstrated to interact with full-length Nup98 in fly (Pascual-Garcia et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Pascual-Garcia et al., 2014).

claim: Nup98-HoxA9 first binds to facultative heterochromatin and then recruits histone and/or chromatin modifying enzymes to induce active histone modifications and a subsequent activation of Hox cluster genes.
source: Thus, we speculate that Nup98-HoxA9 first binds to facultative heterochromatin and then recruits histone and/or chromatin modifying enzymes to induce active histone modifications and a subsequent activation of Hox cluster genes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental observations and cited studies.

claim: In CD133+ hematopoietic stem cells, histone modifications of Hox-A and Hox-B loci are also bivalent.
source: Importantly, in CD133+ hematopoietic stem cells, histone modifications of Hox-A and Hox-B loci are also bivalent (Cui et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Cui et al., 2009).

claim: Hox cluster genes are similarly regulated both in ES and hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: suggesting that Hox cluster genes are similarly regulated both in ES and hematopoietic progenitor cells
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that both cell types have bivalent histone modifications at Hox loci.

claim: Selective activation of Hox genes has been reported in other Nup98-fusions, Nup98-NSD1 and Nup98-Jarid1a, in myeloid progenitor cells.
source: Selective activation of Hox genes has also been reported in other Nup98-fusions, Nup98-NSD1 and Nup98-Jarid1a, in myeloid progenitor cells (Wang et al., 2007, Wang et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Wang et al., 2007, Wang et al., 2009).

claim: Nup98-NSD1 binds to the promoter region of Hox-A cluster genes and modifies histones via its H3K36 methyltransferase activity.
source: Mechanistically, Nup98-NSD1 binds to the promoter region of Hox-A cluster genes and modifies histones via its H3K36 methyltransferase activity (Wang et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Wang et al., 2007).

claim: Nup98-Jarid1a binds to di- or tri-methylated H3K4 of the Hox-A cluster region through its plant homeodomain (PHD) finger domain and causes deregulation of Hox genes activation.
source: Similarly, Nup98-Jarid1a binds to di- or tri-methylated H3K4 of the Hox-A cluster region through its plant homeodomain (PHD) finger domain and causes deregulation of Hox genes activation (Wang et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Wang et al., 2009).

claim: Chromosome prebound Crm1 may recruit Nup98-NSD1, Nup98-Jarid1a, and possibly other Nup98-fusions to specific Hox cluster genes loci through its interaction with the Nup98FG repeat.
source: Our results suggest that chromosome prebound Crm1 may recruit Nup98-NSD1, Nup98-Jarid1a, and possibly other Nup98-fusions to specific Hox cluster genes loci through its interaction with the Nup98FG repeat, which commonly exists in all Nup98-fusions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the current study's findings and knowledge about Nup98-fusions.

claim: Nup98FG could only weakly bind to Hox-A cluster region.
source: Unexpectedly, our data showed that Nup98FG could only weakly bind to Hox-A cluster region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nup98FG is hardly accessible to the genomic DNA, including the Hox cluster region, when expressed by itself.
source: However, since Nup98FG dots are frequently localized within the nucleolus (data not shown), and Nup98FG is more prone to form nuclear aggregates than Nup98-HoxA9 with only a weak nucleoplasmic diffuse staining (see Figure 2B), we speculate that Nup98FG is hardly accessible to the genomic DNA, including the Hox cluster region, when expressed by itself.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed localization patterns.

claim: Crm1 binds to the HoxA9 and HoxA10 gene regions, both in human leukemia cell line and immortalized mouse embryonic fibroblast cell line.
source: Notably, a recent report (Conway et al., 2014) also demonstrated that Crm1 binds to the HoxA9 and HoxA10 gene regions, both in human leukemia cell line and immortalized mouse embryonic fibroblast cell line.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Conway et al., 2014).

claim: Crm1 recruits CALM-AF10 fusion through its interaction with the nuclear export signal on CALM to activate Hox gene expression.
source: Conway et al. (2014) further showed that Crm1 recruits CALM-AF10 fusion through its interaction with the nuclear export signal on CALM to activate Hox gene expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Conway et al., 2014).

claim: The association of Crm1 with Hox loci could be a common molecular basis for aberrant Hox gene dysregulation mediated by numerous leukemic fusions.
source: Thus, the association of Crm1 with Hox loci could be a common molecular basis for aberrant Hox gene dysregulation mediated by numerous leukemic fusions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current study's findings and the cited study (Conway et al., 2014).
